questions.explain: The chapter stresses that revoking a user's privileges while leaving the login intact does not remove access — the user can still connect; dropping a login while users remain creates orphaned users.
options: A revoked login can still execute stored procedures
Orphaned users block the transaction log
Revoking all privileges without removing the login still allows the user to connect; dropping a login leaves orphaned users
Authorization happens before authentication
questions.q: What common mistakes does the chapter warn about when removing someone's database access?

questions.explain: DENY explicitly prohibits an action and takes precedence over any GRANT, even inherited through role membership — but the chapter says to use it sparingly because it makes effective permissions harder to audit.
options: DENY only applies to the public role
DENY takes precedence over any GRANT, even through role membership
DENY cannot be combined with GRANT on the same object
DENY requires sysadmin membership to issue
questions.q: Alice is in the reporting_team role with SELECT on sales.orders, but she has an individual DENY SELECT on that table. What is the result?

questions.explain: The chapter notes that when procedure and tables share an owner, permissions are only checked on the procedure; if ownership differs, the chain breaks and table permissions are re-checked — and WITH EXECUTE AS OWNER procedures with unsanitized dynamic SQL become privilege escalation vectors.
options: Ownership chaining requires RLS to be enabled
Chained procedures always need explicit table grants
Ownership chains only work for column-level permissions

When procedure and tables share an owner, only the procedure's permissions are checked — but a chain break re-checks table permissions, and EXECUTE AS OWNER with dynamic SQL is a privilege escalation risk
questions.q: How does ownership chaining affect permission checks, and what risk does the chapter attach to EXECUTE AS OWNER?

questions.explain: The chapter says TRUSTWORTHY lets code in the database access server-level resources using the database owner's server-level credentials; it is off by default and should stay off in production unless specifically documented.
options: TRUSTWORTHY allows code in a database to use the database owner's server-level credentials, so it should stay off unless specifically documented
TRUSTWORTHY is required for RLS to work
TRUSTWORTHY enables column-level encryption
TRUSTWORTHY disables the guest user
questions.q: Why does the chapter say the TRUSTWORTHY database property should be audited and left off in production?

questions.explain: The chapter warns that revoking CONNECT from guest prevents this; otherwise any authenticated login without an explicit user mapping can connect through guest and receive whatever permissions guest holds.
options: Guest users bypass all RLS policies
The public role cannot be audited
Any authenticated login without an explicit user mapping can connect through guest and inherit its permissions
Guest accounts force snapshot isolation on
questions.q: What is the danger of leaving the guest user enabled in a SQL Server database?
